label: Aortic stenosis
summary: Narrowing of the aortic valve opening, most often from age-related calcification or a bicuspid valve. The LV must generate higher pressure to eject, so it thickens. Once symptoms start, outcomes without valve replacement are poor.

levers.why: The narrowed valve is a fixed obstruction, so the LV must push against a higher pressure.
Higher wall stress and a thickened LV raise myocardial oxygen demand, so angina can occur even with normal coronaries.

nursingPriorities: Treat as preload-dependent: avoid sudden drops in preload, such as rapid diuresis or nitrates, without a provider plan, and report hypotension early.
Report new exertional chest pain, syncope or dyspnea; symptom onset marks severe disease and triggers valve replacement review.
New atrial fibrillation or tachycardia is poorly tolerated, because the stiff LV relies on atrial kick and diastolic filling time; report it promptly.

relations.why: The lesion is the stiff, calcified or malformed valve leaflets.
Turbulent flow across the narrowed valve during ejection makes the murmur.
A fixed outflow limits output with exertion: angina from high O2 demand, syncope from failure to raise output, dyspnea from rising filling pressure.
Slow ejection through the narrowed valve makes the carotid pulse weak and late.
Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis and grades its severity.
Transcatheter replacement treats symptomatic severe AS; the heart team weighs age, surgical risk and anatomy.
Surgical replacement treats symptomatic severe AS, especially in younger or lower-risk patients.
